column4: The section's miser keeps a hand closed; here what they withhold is made into a collar around their necks, turning the closed hand into a burden.
The section sets giving against the miser's withholding; this image says not to bind the hand to the neck or open it without limit, giving the reader both edges and the measured hand between them.
The section says wealth will not help the one who falls; the ruined garden owner turns both palms over what he spent, making the image of the empty hand after loss.

After God gives them of His bounty, these people become stingy and turn away (بخلوا به وتولوا); the paired roots named in the section make this a direct reversal of giving and its freedom from a claimant.
The section says a human favor can become a debt that binds; Moses answers Pharaoh's claim of nurture by naming the enslavement of the Israelites, exposing the coercion behind that claimed favor.
Pharaoh invokes having raised Moses as a child among them (ألم نربك فينا وليدا), a concrete example of the favor a giver may later hold over its recipient; 26:22 supplies Moses' answer.
The section's giver acts for the Lord's face without repaying a human hand; these feeders say they seek neither recompense nor thanks (لا نريد منكم جزاء ولا شكورا), making that motive explicit.
This ayah says charity is spent seeking God's face (ابتغاء وجه الله), the same motive the section assigns to its giver, and locates the gift's purpose beyond settling a human claim.
After giving, these people do not follow their spending with reminders or injury (منا ولا أذى); the section's freed giver likewise does not turn a gift into a debt collectible from its recipient.

The section's cited ع س ر dictionary branch describes demanding a debt from an insolvent person without waiting for ease; this ayah sets the boundary in the opposite direction, ordering delay until ease and saying waiving the debt as charity is better.

Solomon rejects the queen's gift and says what God gave him is better (فما آتاني الله خير مما آتاكم); the human gift cannot bind him to a return, clarifying the section's distinction between God's bounty and an indebted hand.
The section's hand reaches outward to give; these people feed the poor, orphan, and captive out of love for the food, with the next ayah stating their no-recompense motive.
This ayah warns against nullifying charity by reminders and injury (بالمن والأذى); it shows the human claim that the section's giver has no need to collect from beneficiaries.
Kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury (صدقة يتبعها أذى); this sets a gracious response against a gift turned into leverage, as in the section's no-debt giver.

For slaves seeking a written contract, the verse orders the contract and then says to give them from God's wealth (وآتوهم من مال الله); it joins the section's slave's work toward freedom with an actual transfer of wealth.

The section identifies sadaqa as wealth a person gives; this ayah says righteousness requires spending from what one loves, making the gift a real relinquishment rather than payment for a prior favor.

This account of righteousness joins giving wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy, petitioners, and freeing people from bondage (وفي الرقاب), uniting the section's open hand and its image of manumission.
In the law of retaliation, waiving a claim is called charity (فمن تصدق به); the section's gift-without-debt image gains a concrete case where a person gives up an enforceable return.

The section's listed dictionary wording for تمنن is giving while seeking an increase; this command forbids that transactional hand, matching the giver who seeks the Lord's face rather than more from people.

The section notes the root ج ز ي for recompense in both good and evil; this ayah gives its positive side directly, asking whether the recompense of excellence is anything but excellence (جزاء الإحسان إلا الإحسان).
The section's root ج ز ي includes answering good and evil; this ayah makes the boundary explicit, with an evil repaid in kind but forgiveness rewarded by God, beyond a human debt claim.
The section frees its donor from repaying any person's favor; this ayah uses the debt image for a good loan to God (يقرض الله قرضا حسنا), whose return comes from God rather than a human beneficiary.
The section distinguishes giving from settling a human debt; this ayah places charity and a good loan to God together, with God multiplying the return, relocating the creditor relation.
The section's debt world has a human creditor, while this ayah calls giving a good loan to God (يقرض الله قرضا حسنا) and promises its multiplication by Him.
This ayah again calls giving to God a good loan and promises its return multiplied; it clarifies that the section's release from human indebtedness can coexist with trust in God's recompense.
After commanding prayer and zakat, this ayah asks believers to lend God a good loan; its divine recipient gives the section's no-human-debt gift a distinct, promised return.
For accidental killing, this ayah requires freeing a believing slave and sets blood compensation for the family unless they waive it; release, compensation, and waived claim meet in one ruling.
The section's cited dictionary sense defines sadaqa as what one gives from one's self and wealth; here alms are taken from wealth to purify the giver, tying the gift to purification.
This distribution of alms includes freeing people from bondage (وفي الرقاب), showing charity itself directed to the section's image of slavery and release.
The section develops slavery as the most severe bond in the gift world; this ayah names freeing a neck (فك رقبة) as a concrete step on the difficult ascent.
The ascent continues with feeding during a day of hunger (في يوم ذي مسغبة); after 90:13 names freeing a slave, this row adds the costly provision that follows it.
The next detail of the ascent is feeding an orphan who is a relative (يتيما ذا مقربة); it specifies a recipient of the section's giving hand, following 90:14's hunger scene.
The ascent also reaches a poor person in distress (مسكينا ذا متربة); this row specifies another recipient, completing the acts listed after 90:13's freeing of a slave.
This ruling requires freeing a slave as expiation before a husband resumes marital relations after an oath; it shows the concrete release the section places at the center of its slavery image.
Among the expiations for a broken oath is freeing a slave; this is another specific instance of release as an act that discharges an obligation.
The section's giver parts with wealth for God's sake; this ayah stages spending as seed that multiplies many times, showing how a gift's consequence may exceed the amount given.
This command concerns what people give from their earnings and crops, warning them not to select what they themselves would reject; it makes the quality of the giving hand part of the image.
The ayah says public charity is good and concealing it while giving to the poor is better; this makes visible and hidden forms of the section's giving hand legible.
Those who spend their wealth by night and day, privately and publicly, are promised reward; the verse makes explicit that the hand's giving is not confined to one occasion or manner.
This ayah contrasts God's increase of charity (يربي الصدقات) with the erasure of usury, distinguishing a gift from wealth put to work for a financial return.
The verse contrasts usury, which does not increase with God, with zakat given seeking God's face; that distinction sharpens the section's separation of charitable giving from a human debt or claim.
These worshippers spend from what God provided and hope for a trade that will not fail (تجارة لن تبور); their spiritual return clarifies the section's giver's relation to God.
The next ayah says God will give them their rewards in full and increase them from His bounty; it supplies the divine return behind 35:29's unperishing trade.
This ayah says whatever is spent, God replaces it and is the best provider; it makes God's provision, rather than repayment from the human recipient, the giver's horizon.
Believers are told to spend from what God has made them successors over; the wealth's prior source and temporary custody illuminate why the section's donor need not collect a human debt.
The praised people spend from what God provided, both secretly and openly, and repel evil with good; this pairs the section's gift with a response that does not keep score.
The section's dictionary image treats blessing as a hand; this prayer locates all good in God's hand (بيدك الخير) and says He gives and withholds rule, framing the ultimate giver.
The verse says God's bounty is in His control and that He gives it to whom He wills; it anchors the section's “blessing as hand” image in God's unowed generosity.
When believers are asked to spend, the stingy are told their withholding harms themselves and that God is rich while they are needy; this reverses the section's open hand and self-sufficient miser.
This ayah names those who are stingy and turn away (يبخلون ... ومن يتول); it brings together the section's two roots for the withholding hand and the one who turns away.
The verse describes misers who hide what God gave them of His bounty; it links the section's closed hand with concealing a gift whose source lies beyond the recipient.
Believers are told to spend for their own good and guard against their own miserliness; the section's stingy hand is thus a loss to its holder, not a debt avoided.

The Helpers give the emigrants priority over themselves even in hardship, and the verse says those protected from their own avarice succeed; it shows the freedom on the far side of the section's closed hand.

The verse pictures those given more provision refusing to share it with people their right hands possess; that unequal hand relation illuminates the section's link between wealth, ownership, and bondage.
A due share in the wealthy person's property is assigned to the petitioner and deprived person; this gives the asking hand in the section a recognized place in the giver's wealth.
The verse says a known share is kept in the wealth of those who pray; it presents provision for others as part of possessing wealth, not a favor that creates a personal debt.
The next ayah identifies the recipients of that share as the petitioner and deprived person; it completes 70:24's claim with the two hands that meet in the section's scene.

This ayah identifies needy people who cannot travel for livelihood and do not persistently ask others; it helps the reader see that the section's asking hand belongs to real need, not an abstract word.
The command not to repel a petitioner (السائل فلا تنهر) directly answers the section's dictionary scene of someone asking people with an outstretched palm.
The queen says she will send Solomon a gift and see what the envoys return; the next ayah reveals the gift's transactional test, meeting the section's image of a hand that expects repayment.
These people vow that if God gives them bounty they will give charity; 9:76 shows that after receiving it they withhold it, so this row supplies the promise that the neighboring reversal breaks.
This ayah says hypocrisy was placed in their hearts because they broke their promise to God and lied; following 9:76's stingy turning away, it shows the consequence of the failed pledge.
The command to spend comes before a day with no sale or friendship (لا بيع فيه ولا خلة); as in the section, wealth's human exchange value cannot help at the final reckoning.
This ayah commands spending from God's provision before the day with no trade or friendship; it repeats 2:254's final deadline while linking it directly to provision and giving.
Believers are told to spend from God's provision before death arrives, when a person will wish for delay; this makes the section's useless wealth at the fall an urgent reason to give.
The condemned speaker says his wealth did not avail him (ما أغنى عني ماليه); this is the section's claim about wealth at the moment of collapse in another voice.
The ayah says no offered compensation will be accepted from the soul facing judgment; it extends the section's warning that wealth cannot buy release at the end.
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God's way embody the section's closed hand; the next ayah describes the consequence, while this one identifies the withheld wealth.
The servants' spending is neither excessive nor miserly but balanced; this states the middle measure between the two hand positions set out in the section.
The verse criticizes people who spend their wealth to be seen by others; this distinguishes the section's giver seeking God's face from a hand opened for public credit.
The section notes that the root ء ت ي can mean giving and also bringing something; the knowledgeable one says he will bring the throne to Solomon, joining gift-like transfer to physical arrival.

The verse says God and the Prophet both bestowed favor on Zayd (أنعم الله عليه وأنعمت عليه); though its immediate issue is his marriage, it recalls the section's former slave whose relation to his benefactors is described through favor.
The section's dictionary entry names نعمة as a hand or benefaction; this ayah says every blessing people have comes from God, shifting the source of the “hand” away from a human creditor.
The passage calls faith and striving a trade that saves from painful punishment; this makes explicit the spiritual-exchange language behind the section's giver who acts for the Lord's face.
The next ayah specifies that this trade involves striving with wealth and lives in God's way; it gives the concrete expenditure behind 61:10's image of trade.

A speaker boasts that he has spent abundant wealth (أهلكت مالا لبدا); the next ascent passage names freeing a slave and feeding the hungry, distinguishing display of expenditure from the section's beneficial open hand.
The verse says that even all the earth's wealth could not ransom those facing punishment; it gives a concrete limit to the section's claim that wealth cannot save its owner at the fall.

The verse answers the claim that God's hand is chained by saying His hands are spread wide and He gives as He wills; this extends the section's tight and open hand image to the contrast between a human giver and the unbounded divine giver.
The hypocrites are described as holding their hands back; this makes the section's miser's closed hand a concrete act of withholding, tied to forgetting God.

The section's dictionary branch for wrongful reaching means taking what one has no right to; this verse forbids consuming others' wealth falsely and using judges to seize it, giving that grasping hand a specific legal form.

The section distinguishes a rightful gift from taking what is not one's right; this verse forbids wrongful appropriation but permits trade by mutual consent, marking the boundary between a grasping hand and a lawful exchange.
Guardians are told to hand orphans their property and not substitute bad for good or consume it; this gives the section's rightful giving and wrongful reaching an exact setting of entrusted wealth.
Those who consume orphans' property unjustly are warned they consume fire; this is a concrete instance of the section's dictionary sense of reaching for what is not rightfully yours.
The verse forbids restricting wives in order to take back part of what was given to them; it shows a prior gift being turned into a claim against its recipient.
Even a great amount given to a wife may not be taken back when a husband replaces her; this is a direct boundary against treating a gift as a recoverable debt.

The verse forbids taking back what was given to a wife, with a stated exception when she gives compensation to secure release from the marriage; it marks the specific boundary between a gift and a negotiated return.
The section describes the miser as one who considers himself self-sufficient; this verse uses the same self-sufficiency wording for the person whose false independence leads to transgression.
This passage turns to the one who sees himself as self-sufficient (استغنى), the same posture named in the section's miser, and shows whom the addressed figure favors.

The arriving man's possible self-purification is raised here; it meets the section's donor who gives wealth to purify himself, while 80:2 identifies the visitor whose potential benefit was overlooked.
The person who comes striving (يسعى) is the other side of the section's divided striving; this ayah introduces the seeker whose fear is named in 80:9.
This ayah says the striving visitor is fearful; it echoes the section's giver who fears God, and 80:8 supplies the distinct act of striving.
The section identifies the turning-away root and the asking hand; here the addressed figure turns away as a visitor arrives, placing refusal beside a person who has come seeking attention.
This ayah identifies the visitor as a blind man; it supplies the human need behind the turning-away in 80:1, though he comes seeking attention rather than a stated monetary gift.
The addressed figure attends to the self-sufficient man; after 80:5 identifies his posture, this ayah shows the social preference opposite the section's open hand to a needy recipient.
The addressed figure is distracted from the striving visitor; this completes the turning-away scene begun in 80:1 and contrasts with the section's attention to giving and striving.

The visitor might take heed and benefit from a reminder; this ayah gives a possible outcome for the seeker whose purification is raised in 80:3, echoing the section's concern with the one who fears and believes.

The verse says the addressed figure is not responsible if the self-sufficient man does not purify himself; it qualifies 80:6's attention to him, while the section grounds purification in the giver's own act rather than a return extracted from someone else.
This ayah says the human being transgresses; 96:7 gives the reason as seeing himself self-sufficient, matching the section's self-sufficient miser as the moral danger.
The passage rebukes people for not honoring the orphan; this is a concrete failure of the giving hand to the vulnerable, rather than a lack of wealth alone.
The passage adds that they do not encourage feeding the poor; this follows the failure to honor the orphan and names another recipient of the section's charitable hand.
The people consume inheritance greedily; this is a concrete wrongful taking of another's due, matching the section's secondary sense of reaching for what is not one's right.
The passage says people love wealth intensely; this gives the inward attachment behind the section's miserly hand a direct formulation.

The person treats abundant provision as proof that God has honored him; this begins the passage's rebuke of reading wealth as self-sufficiency, which 89:17-20 connects to neglect of the vulnerable and love of wealth.
When provision is restricted, the person calls it humiliation; beside 89:15, this shows the mistaken reading of wealth and scarcity that the passage answers with duties toward the orphan and poor.
Satan threatens poverty while God promises forgiveness and bounty; this names the fear of scarcity that closes the hand and contrasts it with trust in the giver's bounty.
The women are to receive their marriage-gifts as a gracious giving, and may remit some only willingly; this separates a freely ceded gift from an amount a recipient is forced to return.
The verse invokes the solemn covenant between spouses as the reason taking back the gift is grave; it completes 4:20's direct prohibition with the relationship that makes the return a betrayal.
Guardians must return orphans' wealth when they are ready and may not consume it wastefully or hastily; the verse distinguishes a rightful handover from a custodian's attempt to take what is not his.

The section describes a world of actual debts and claims; this verse concerns a real debt for a fixed term and orders it written fairly, helping distinguish a contractual liability from the section's freely given wealth.
The verse calls Allah the Mawla of believers and says disbelievers have no Mawla; it gives the section's patron and benefactor word a divine referent beyond a human bond of indebtedness.
If people turn away, this verse names Allah as their Mawla; it brings together the section's turning-away verb and its dictionary branch for a patron or benefactor.
Allah is the believers' Wali and brings them from darkness into light; this makes the section's patron word an active liberating relation, not a human claim to repayment.
The righteous spend in both ease and hardship, restrain anger, and pardon people; this joins the section's giving hand with a response that releases a claim rather than demanding its return.
Neither wealth nor children will avail those facing God; this is another explicit boundary on the property that the section says cannot help its owner at the fall.
On the Day when neither wealth nor children avail, the section's warning about wealth failing at the end is stated directly.

The next ayah says only one who comes to God with a sound heart is saved; it supplies the inward condition against which 26:88's useless wealth is measured, recalling the section's giving to purify oneself.
The section's dictionary gloss for ج ز ي includes repayment for good and evil; this verse says God repays those who do wrong and those who do good, specifying both sides of that meaning.
The verse says an evil is repaid only with its like, while a believing doer of good receives more than a simple worldly balance; it develops the section's two directions of recompense.

This ayah depicts God as purchasing the believers' lives and wealth in exchange for Paradise; it clarifies the section's giving for God's face as an exchange with God, not repayment to a human benefactor.
The next ayah names forgiveness and gardens as the reward for the trade introduced in 61:10 and specified by spending wealth in 61:11; it gives the divine return behind that exchange.
This ayah says the one who purifies himself succeeds; it makes explicit the self-purification named in the section's description of the giver's wealth.
The verse says the soul succeeds when purified; it clarifies that the section's giving wealth to purify oneself concerns moral purification of the self.
